works.abstract: Food packaging (FP) is essential for preserving food quality, safety, and extending shelf-life. However, growing concerns about the environmental and health impacts of conventional packaging materials, particularly per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and microplastics, are driving a major transformation in FP design. PFAS, synthetic compounds with dual hydro- and lipophobicity, have been widely employed in food packaging materials (FPMs) to impart desirable water and grease repellency. However, PFAS bioaccumulate in the human body and have been linked to multiple health effects, including immune system dysfunction, cancer, and developmental problems. The detection of microplastics in various FPMs has raised significant concerns regarding their potential migration into food and subsequent ingestion. This comprehensive review examines the current landscape of FPMs, their functions, and physicochemical properties to put into perspective why there is widespread use of PFAS and microplastics in FPMs. The review then addresses the challenges posed by PFAS and microplastics, emphasizing the urgent need for sustainable and bio-based alternatives. We highlight promising advancements in sustainable and renewable materials, including plant-derived polysaccharides, proteins, and waxes, as well as recycled and upcycled materials. The integration of these sustainable materials into active packaging systems is also examined, indicating innovations in oxygen scavengers, moisture absorbers, and antimicrobial packaging. The review concludes by identifying key research gaps and future directions, including the need for comprehensive life cycle assessments and strategies to improve scalability and cost-effectiveness. As the FP industry evolves, a holistic approach considering environmental impact, functionality, and consumer acceptance will be crucial in developing truly sustainable packaging solutions.
works.journal: Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety
works.title: Food packaging solutions in the post‐per‐ and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and microplastics era: A review of functions, materials, and bio‐based alternatives

works.abstract: Microbial contamination, cross-contamination, and biofilm formation on abiotic food-contact equipment and biotic food surfaces remain leading causes of foodborne illness and post-harvest food loss worldwide. Conventional chemical sanitation and thermal clean-in-place (CIP) protocols face persistent limitations once bacterial cells anchor within surface microcrevices and secrete protective extracellular polymeric substances (EPS). Superhydrophobic coatings—engineered through the synergy of low surface energy and hierarchical micro/nanoscale roughness to stabilize a Cassie–Baxter composite solid–liquid–vapor interface—offer a fundamentally distinct, physics-driven line of defense. Rather than relying solely on chemical eradication, these surfaces maintain an interfacial air cushion (plastron) that restricts true solid–liquid contact area, elevates free-energy barriers to bacterial adhesion, attenuates attractive Lifshitz–van der Waals interactions, amplifies hydrodynamic slip, and promotes low-shear self-cleaning. This review synthesizes the multiscale biophysics governing bacterial repellency on superhydrophobic interfaces in food systems, integrating recent post-2024 advances in wetting thermodynamics, gas-permeability-controlled plastron dissolution kinetics, non-mean-field interfacial electrostatics, turbulent slip nonlocality, flow-coupled active bacterial hydrodynamics, droplet impact kinematics, and lipid–membrane biophysics. Particular attention is given to how amphiphilic food lipids, proteins, and surfactants adsorb onto the air–water meniscus, alter interfacial dilatational rheology and line tension, and dictate the finite Cassie-to-Wenzel transition time beyond static water contact angles. We establish a mechanistic taxonomy of five major coating design architectures—nanotextured and nanodiamond-reinforced metals, silica aerogels and optically transparent topographies, polymeric food-contact and post-PFAS cellulosic substrates, edible wax/triterpenoid/lipid-derived produce coatings, and dual-functional or stimuli-responsive "defense-in-depth" systems—benchmarked against slippery liquid-infused and covalently attached liquid-like surfaces. Finally, we critically evaluate translational barriers—including mechanical abrasion, CIP durability, cold-chain micro-condensation, splash-mediated aerosol cross-contamination, nanoparticle and micro/nanoplastic migration, and landmark 2025–2026 regulatory mandates (US FDA PFAS phase-outs and EU Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation [PPWR] fluorine limits)—and outline a strategic roadmap toward durable, fluorine-free, AI-designed hygienic biointerfaces.
works.title: Biophysics and Biochemistry of Superhydrophobic Coatings for Microbiological Hygiene on Food and Food-Contact Surfaces: Mechanisms, Coating Architectures, and Translational Outlook
